messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Using seewave for microphone calibration testing
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] Using seewave for microphone calibration testing
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stefanie,

Regarding the first option you proposed (using spec()) do you know how to transform the amplitude by frequency values according to the microphone sensitivity? In other words, which is the scale of the obtained amplitude values using spec() with the argument norm=FALSE?

Many thanks in advance for your assistance,

Irene

On Thursday, May 11, 2017 at 9:38:52 AM UTC-4, Stefanie LaZerte wrote:
>
> Off the top of my head (and not as an expert) I would suggest using the spec() function with the argument norm = FALSE (i.e. don't normalize the amplitude data). This provides a frequency spectrum of amplitude by frequency. If you don't normalize the data and if you use a calibration tool, I think you should be able to compare the 40 kHz amplitude peaks.
>
> Alternatively you could filter to a narrow band around 40kHz and use env() to calculate the amplitude envelope, and then take the root-mean-square to get an average amplitude at 40kHz.
>
> It depends also on whether you simply want to compare the microphones, or whether you want to have concrete statistics about each one (comparisons are much easier).
>
> Good luck!
>
> Steffi
> Dr. Stefanie LaZerte
> stefanie...@unbc.ca
> http://steffi.ca/
> On 2017-05-11 10:22 AM, Alison Fairbrass wrote:
> > Dear SeeWave users,
> >
> > I would like to test some ultrasonic microphones in terms of a number of factors such as their detection distance, sensitivity deterioration and orientation in relation to sound source. I plan to use a calibration tool which emits a sound at a set frequency of 40 kHz in this testing.
> >
> > I plan to test the difference between recordings by comparing the power of the signal recorded at 40 kHz. Are there any functions in seewave that enable you to measure signal power at a defined frequency or within a defined frequency band? Or, are there better measures you would suggest to conduct this testing that can be calculated using seewave?
> >
> > Many thanks in advance for your assistance,
> > Alison

messages.subject: Filtering changes gain?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I just found found something rather peculiar - not sure whether I don't understand the basics of this or there is some hidden normalisation. Basically, when I create a spectrogram of the original file, the amplitude is fine.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-KgDCh35k2j8/Wl8ttr-1iSI/AAAAAAAAIC8/GK_sW3MPLEoeAUJjfK3aeq75QjOtJl2NQCLcBGAs/s1600/Rplot09.png>
When I apply a low-pass filter to get rid of wind noise, the amplitude gets massively boosted...

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/--QfQHUwPvxk/Wl8t_n4eJyI/AAAAAAAAIDA/T9NL8Rx518ArMjVsNEasbjL3jJjcGjTKQCLcBGAs/s1600/Rplot08.png>
File is attached and code is below -- any clues?
Simon
----------------------------------

normal<-readWave("rs03_20091001_055000.wav")
spectro(normal, collevels=seq(-60,0,1),  wl=512, palette= color.palette,  f=freq)

normalfilt<-ffilter(normal,f=freq,from=1000)
spectro(normalfilt, collevels=seq(-60,0,1),  wl=512, palette= color.palette,  f=freq)

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Filtering changes gain?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Simon,
Yes, the amplitude values are lost, this is due to the use of the STFT and iSTFT.
There will be a new argument in the next version of seewave to try to get similar values than the input signal.
This should happen soon (package submitted yesterday but there is a bug I cannot fix - CRAN Core team is helping).
Best
Jerome

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Filtering changes gain?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jerome! Thanks!

What does that mean for calculating M, H and ACI?
So here comes the full story:

I am trying to calculate M, H and ACI for 7900 files and noticed that I have too much noise below 1kHz (rain, wind, cars). So I applied the high pass filter in seewave and calculated M. Only when I plotted some example spectrograms as a last step for the paper I noticed the change in amplitude.
So I take it the numeric value of M is also changed (although it is pretty small)?

2 questions:
1. Is M changed proportionally for all of the files - in which case at least my conclusions don't change - or does it depend on the amplitude of the filtered bits?
2. Is there any way that I can filter and preserve the the amplitude of the non-filtered bits?

Simon

Simon

if I give it the full path C:\\Work\\BioRcoustic\\Flows\\Origfiles\\ it works - somehow R doesn't find drives that are mounted as a drive in Windows!
Simon
